topic: Design a skill for watching up-and-coming/underground Roblox games with potential, via YouTube, TikTok and similar sources
initialPrompt:

qAndA.question: D1 — Skill mechanics mirror the daily-trends-report pattern: manual invocation, home in .agents/skills/, built to write-a-skill-v2 conventions, runtime harness opencode, research orchestrated on the existing fleet (b0tts-lead-researcher → b0tts-researcher leaves → b0tts-smart-general-agent writer), no new agent definitions. Exact skill name/output paths decided later once the purpose is settled.

D2 — Design independence: the new skill is designed from scratch, not built on daily-trends-report's scripts. That build is mid-flight (S1–S6 unfinished, scripts never executed), so its machinery is not a dependable foundation to copy. We borrow the pattern, not the code. This session designs; building happens later as its own effort.

Q1 — Why do you want to find these games? What is the report FOR?

"Potential" only means something relative to a goal, and the goal changes what the skill tracks and how the report reads. From your project I can see you build Roblox games (the retention-brainstorm skill) and do viral-video research (viral-shortvideo-frameworks, viral-lyric-workflows), so a few guesses:

- (a) Dev research — find underground games to learn from: mechanics, retention loops, monetization worth borrowing for your own game before they go mainstream
- (b) Content creation — find games to make YouTube/TikTok videos about while they're still undiscovered
- (c) Playing — just want to know what's cool to play before everyone else
- (d) Something else I'm not seeing

My recommendation: (a) — you build Roblox games, and "games that have potential" is exactly the kind of signal a dev wants (early proof a loop works before the crowd shows up). But if you're scouting video topics, (b) changes the whole shape of the report.
qAndA.answer: a and c. mainly for a though.

qAndA.question:
Q2 — How often should this run?

The daily-trends-report is daily because AI news genuinely turns over every day — it has a 15-minute daily ritual slot built for it. Underground Roblox games move slower: a game that's "up and coming" stays interesting for weeks, and a daily scan would re-serve the same handful of games over and over.

- (a) Daily — same rhythm as daily-trends-report; the skill then needs heavy freshness machinery to avoid repetition
- (b) Weekly — one scan a week; matches how game momentum actually builds; new picks + movement updates each week
- (c) On-demand — no fixed cadence, you invoke it whenever you want a scan

My recommendation: (b) weekly. "Watching" a game rise is a weekly-timescale thing — a game needs days-to-weeks of data before growth means anything, and a weekly report gives each game room to move between reports. Daily would burn your attention on noise.
qAndA.answer: a daily. However i'm fine with daily being kinda stale, so we can kinda put more emphasis on the redundant section, and make it like a normal section.

qAndA.question:
Q3 — How should the skill remember games between runs?

daily-trends-report treats repetition as a defect: it keeps a 2-day memory and DEMOTES anything that reappears into a cramped "Still circulating" corner. You're saying the opposite — repeats are fine, even welcome. Two architectures handle that:

- (a) Watchlist model — a persistent list file (the skill's own state, e.g. watchlist.json) that tracks every game across runs: when it was first spotted, its stats at each run (players, favorites, views), and a movement verdict (rising / holding / cooling / dead). Each daily report = New picks today + the full watchlist with movement. Games stay visible as long as they're alive; they age out when they stagnate. This is a trend TRACKER — the same game appearing day after day with growing numbers is the whole point.
- (b) Digest model (like daily-trends-report) — each day is a fresh scan; a game can appear at most twice before being demoted. To honor your "stale is fine" answer, the demoted pile becomes a normal, full-size section instead of a cramped corner.

My recommendation: (a). Your daily + stale-ok answers describe a tracker, not a digest. With (a), a game rising from 200 → 800 players across a week IS the report — the persistence is the value. With (b) the skill still fights its own memory every run, and you'd be reading the same game re-described as "new" by different sources.
qAndA.answer:
a watchlist model

Also heres what i mean by underground:
Growth Spike — Rapidly increasing player count (e.g., jumped from 500 to 3K in a day)
Creator Buzz — Small/mid-tier YouTubers or TikTokers covering the game
Veteran Dev — Built by a developer with a track record of previous hits
Community Hype — Gaining traction in niche communities (Twitter threads, small Discord servers)
Viral Moment — A specific clip, meme, or moment is spreading organically
Update Wave — A major update just dropped and early reactions are strong
must have under 10k ccu. Dont look at peaks, focus on avg throughout a timespan. I want realistic data.

qAndA.question: D3 — Signal taxonomy locked (from user's Q3 answer): a game qualifies as underground only with CCU under 10k, measured by average across a timespan, never peak. Six signals: Growth Spike, Creator Buzz, Veteran Dev, Community Hype, Viral Moment, Update Wave. Every signal claim in a report must carry a source link and a dated, verifiable number from platform/tracker data — never a number restated from a social post without the platform page behind it.

D4 — Veteran Dev detection: a creator's track record is checked on their roblox.com profile page, which lists their other published games with visit counts. Previous hit = prior game with a large visit count relative to its age. No API key needed; page is fetchable.

Q4 (re-asked) — Set the three watchlist knobs as one package: intake, cap, and patience (how long a stagnant game stays before it's cut).

- (a) Tight — up to 2-3 new picks/run, cap ~10, patience ~5-7 days of no movement. Small, fast-moving list; strong signal only; risks cutting a slow-building winner.
- (b) Balanced — up to 5 new picks/run, cap ~15-20, patience ~10-14 days. Roughly 35 candidates/week, ~20 surviving games at a time, each game gets ~1.5-2 weeks to prove movement before it ages out. Matches how game momentum actually builds.
- (c) Loose — up to 10 new picks/run, cap ~30, patience ~3 weeks. Broad net, longer memories, but a long daily read and duds linger.

My recommendation: (b). It's the only package where a game can sit through a full quiet week AND still get cut when it's clearly dead — and the daily read stays scannable. (a) punishes slow risers; (c) turns the report into a chore.

Q5 — Which sources are the backbone vs. the discovery layer?

Your six signals need data, and the sources break into two tiers by reliability:

Platform data (the backbone — real numbers, fetchable pages):
- Roblox game pages — live CCU, favorites, visits, likes/dislikes, last-updated
- RoMonitor / RTrack — third-party trackers with CCU charts and averages over time (your avg-not-peak rule needs these)
- Creator profile pages — the Veteran Dev check (visit counts on their past games)

Discovery sources (where candidates get FOUND):
- YouTube search (roblox + keywords like "new", "underrated", "update") — works fine via web search + reading video pages/transcripts
- TikTok — honest reality check: TikTok blocks most scraping; agents can't reliably search or read TikTok pages. The realistic play is: TikTok content surfaces via web search snippets/embeds of viral TikToks, or by searching what people repost about TikTok trends on X/YouTube. Direct TikTok browsing isn't dependable.
- X/Twitter threads, r/roblox + niche subreddits, Discord chatter (via web search for what's being talked about)

My recommendation: platform data is the mandatory backbone — every game on the watchlist has its CCU average verified there, full stop. Socials are the discovery layer that FEEDS candidates, and no social-sourced number gets into the report without a platform/tracker page behind it. TikTok specifically: best-effort via search snippets and reposts, not direct browsing. YouTube is a first-class discovery source since your Creator Buzz and Viral Moment signals live there.

Q6 — What happens when a game leaves the watchlist? There are two exit paths, and they deserve different treatment.

PATH 1 — Graduation: a game's avg CCU crosses 10k (no longer underground). This is the skill SUCCEEDING — it found a winner early. Options:

- (a) Hard cut — game disappears from the watchlist, no ceremony. Clean, but you lose the proof the skill works.
- (b) Graduated line — the day's report carries a one-line "Graduated" entry (game, first-spotted date, CCU at first spot → CCU now, days on watchlist), then the game is removed. You get the "we called it" receipt exactly once, on the day it happens.
- (c) Persistent graduated log — like (b), but every graduation is also appended to a small persistent list (hall of fame) so you can look back at the skill's hit rate over months.

My recommendation: (b) or (c). A hard cut throws away the only feedback signal that tells you the watchlist is picking real winners — and for dev research, "we spotted it at 400 CCU, it hit 10k three weeks later" is the single most valuable line the report can produce. (c) costs almost nothing extra since the state file already exists.

PATH 2 — Age-out: a game stagnates past the ~10-14 day patience window and gets cut. Options:

- (a) Silent drop — gone from the report, no mention.
- (b) Footer line — the day's report ends with "Aged out: Game A (14d, flat), Game B (12d, cooling)" so you can veto a cut that feels wrong.

My recommendation: (b). Silent drops mean you'll never notice a bad cut — and with 15-20 games on the list, a game drifting sideways can absolutely be misread as dead. One footer line per cut is cheap.

Also worth settling: what COUNTS as crossing 10k — a single day's average above 10k, or something sustained (e.g., 2+ consecutive days) to avoid whipsawing when a game pokes over the line once and falls back? My recommendation: 2+ consecutive days above 10k avg — matches your avg-not-peak discipline.
qAndA.answer: id say b, however lets bake into the skill to remind me to clean up the watchlist every now and then to prevent bloat. Ill hard cut manually.

qAndA.question:
Q6b — What counts as a game crossing 10k avg CCU and triggering graduation?

A game that pokes over 10k once and falls back is still underground in spirit — it had a spike, not a move. Your avg-not-peak discipline suggests a sustained threshold:

- (a) Single day — any one day with avg CCU above 10k graduates it. Simplest, but a one-day hype spike (TikTok moment) would trigger a false graduation, and the game re-enters as "new" later if it cools off.
- (b) 2+ consecutive days above 10k avg — a real move, matches the signal discipline.
- (c) N-of-last-5 days above 10k avg — tolerant of tracker gaps (RTrack/RoMonitor sometimes miss a day) while still requiring sustained movement.

My recommendation: (c) with N=3 — 3 of the last 5 recorded days above 10k avg. It handles the reality that third-party trackers occasionally skip a day, while still demanding the game actually MOVED, not spiked.

Q7 — What is the report's shape? Your watchlist model is a TRACKER, not a digest, so the daily report is a snapshot of movement. Three candidate shapes:

- (a) Tracker-first — sections: ① New picks today (up to 5, each with which of the 6 signals it hit + source links + first-seen avg CCU) → ② The Watchlist (the star section: one table, every active game, columns = days on list, avg CCU now, Δ since yesterday, Δ since first-seen, signals present, movement verdict Rising/Holding/Cooling) → ③ Graduated today (one-liners) → ④ Cleanup candidates (stagnant past patience, manual cut reminder). The table IS the report.
- (b) Story-first — a short prose lede ("3 risers, 1 new pick, watchlist at 14/20") above the same table, for when you're skimming on a busy day.
- (c) Minimal — just the table + one-line new picks; nothing else.

My recommendation: (a), with (b)'s lede as a 1-2 line glance block at the top — a glance block is a sentence, not a section.

Also the disk layout. Sibling uses day folders (YYYY-MM-DD/report.md) under a topic folder + index.md upsert. For a tracker there's an alternative:

- (a) Day folders mirroring the sibling — every day gets its own report.md snapshot; index.md points to the latest; full history preserved. Watchlist state lives in a separate watchlist.json (skill's own state file).
- (b) Single rolling report.md overwritten every run — always exactly one file; history only via the state file. Simpler but you lose the day-by-day paper trail of movement.

My recommendation: (a). Your whole value proposition is movement over time — the day folders ARE the proof, and it matches the reports you already read. State file holds the watchlist; each day's report is a frozen snapshot.
